name: Institutional Knowledge Graphs
title: Institutional Knowledge Graphs
answer: Institutional knowledge graphs are structured representations of an organization's entities, documents, people, projects, datasets, and their relationships, maintained by a university, library, or research institute. They turn scattered institutional records into a queryable network so that researchers and administrators can find connections across grants, publications, equipment, and expertise. The scope typically covers research outputs, funding, organizational units, and the semantic links between them, often aligned with persistent identifiers and controlled vocabularies. Unlike a general web search index, an institutional knowledge graph is curated to reflect the institution's own authoritative sources and internal context.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Institutional knowledge graphs are structured representations of an organization's entities, documents, people, projects, datasets, and their relationships, maintained by a university, library, or research institute. They turn scattered institutional records into a queryable network so that researchers and administrators can find connections across grants, publications, equipment, and expertise. The scope typically covers research outputs, funding, organizational units, and the semantic links between them, often aligned with persistent identifiers and controlled vocabularies. Unlike a general web search index, an institutional knowledge graph is curated to reflect the institution's own authoritative sources and internal context.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Institutional knowledge graphs usually run on graph databases or RDF triple stores, with data ingested from institutional repositories, HR systems, grant management platforms, and library catalogues. The infrastructure includes extract-transform-load pipelines, identifier resolution services, and a query layer such as SPARQL or Cypher. Many deployments use open source graph engines and keep the graph behind an internal API so that downstream applications can read it without direct database access. Storage is often paired with a document or relational system for source records, while the graph holds the normalized relationships.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Building an institutional knowledge graph starts with mapping institutional data sources to a shared ontology or schema, then extracting entities and relationships through a mix of automated parsing and manual curation. Entity resolution links the same person, project, or publication across systems using ORCID, DOIs, internal IDs, and name disambiguation. The graph is maintained through scheduled updates and review workflows, with provenance recorded for each claim so that a statement can be traced to its source record. Validation against controlled vocabularies and domain rules keeps the graph consistent as new data arrives.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Institutional knowledge graphs raise questions about data ownership, access control, and the accuracy of inferred relationships. Because the graph combines personnel, financial, and research data, access is usually role-based and limited to what a person is allowed to see in the underlying systems. Provenance is critical: every edge should carry its source and timestamp so that errors can be corrected and contested claims can be audited. Institutions also need to handle privacy obligations, retention limits, and the risk that an automated link between a person and a sensitive project is wrong or misleading.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Institutional knowledge graphs are moving toward more automated construction from unstructured text such as grant narratives, theses, and internal reports, with human review focused on high-risk edges. They are increasingly being connected across institutions through shared identifiers and federated queries, which could support cross-institutional research discovery without centralizing the data. As language models become more common, the graph is likely to serve as a grounded, citable layer that reduces hallucination by supplying verified institutional facts. The long-term direction is a living research record that links people, outputs, and funding in a way that is machine-readable and auditable.
